summary.text: Take the squarefree composite \(n=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\), whose factors are distinct primes. Using \(P(n)=\prod_{p\mid n}(2p-1)\), one obtains \(P(n)=610815156979325\) and \(P(n)+1=26n\), so \(\gcd(n,P(n)+1)=n\) and hence \(a(n)=1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\gcd(k,m)
\]
be Pillai’s arithmetical function. Then the sequence in the conjecture is
\[
a(m)=\frac{m}{\gcd(m,P(m)+1)}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite positive integer \(n\) for which \(P(n)+1\) is divisible by \(n\). For such an \(n\),
\(\gcd(n,P(n)+1)=n\), and consequently \(a(n)=n/n=1\).

The counterexample is
\[
 n=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341
   =23492890653051.
\]
We first establish the formula used to evaluate \(P(n)\), then verify the required primality and arithmetic facts.

### 1. A divisor formula for the gcd-sum

For every positive integer \(m\),
\[
P(m)=\sum_{d\mid m} d\,\varphi(m/d),
\tag{1}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler’s totient function.

Indeed, group the integers \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq m\) according to the value
\(d=\gcd(k,m)\). Such a value \(d\) must divide \(m\). If \(d\mid m\), write
\(k=dj\). The condition \(\gcd(k,m)=d\) is then equivalent to
\[
1\leq j\leq m/d
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd(j,m/d)=1.
\]
There are exactly \(\varphi(m/d)\) such values of \(j\), including the case
\(m/d=1\). Every member of this class contributes \(d\) to the gcd-sum, so the
class contributes \(d\varphi(m/d)\). Summing over all divisors \(d\) proves
(1).

Formula (1) also shows that \(P\) is multiplicative on coprime arguments. More
precisely, if \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime positive integers, every divisor of
\(uv\) has a unique form \(ef\), where \(e\mid u\) and \(f\mid v\). Moreover,
\(u/e\) and \(v/f\) are coprime. Hence, using the multiplicativity of Euler’s
totient on coprime arguments,
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(uv)
 &=\sum_{e\mid u}\sum_{f\mid v}
       ef\,\varphi\!\left(\frac{u}{e}\frac{v}{f}\right)\\
 &=\sum_{e\mid u}\sum_{f\mid v}
       \left(e\varphi(u/e)\right)
       \left(f\varphi(v/f)\right)\\
 &=P(u)P(v).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

If \(p\) is prime, its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Thus (1) gives
\[
P(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1.
\tag{3}
\]
It follows from (2) and (3) that whenever \(m\) is a product of distinct primes,
\[
P(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}(2p-1).
\tag{4}
\]

### 2. Primality of the factors

We now verify that all five displayed factors of \(n\) are distinct primes.
The primality of \(3,37,43\) is immediate by trial division: for \(37\) and
\(43\), it suffices to test the primes \(2,3,5\), since their square roots are
less than \(7\), and none divides either number.

For completeness, the primality of the two larger numbers can be established
compactly by Lucas’s primality criterion. We use the following standard form of
that criterion.

Suppose \(N>1\), the complete prime factorization of \(N-1\) is known, and an
integer \(b\) satisfies
\[
b^{N-1}\equiv1\pmod N
\]
and, for every distinct prime \(q\mid N-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(N-1)/q}-1,N\bigr)=1.
\tag{5}
\]
Then \(N\) is prime. To see why, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(N\). The
multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(r\) divides \(N-1\). Condition (5) says
that this order does not divide \((N-1)/q\) for any prime \(q\mid N-1\).
Therefore the order contains the full power of every prime occurring in
\(N-1\), and hence the order is exactly \(N-1\). On the other hand, the order
modulo the prime \(r\) divides \(r-1\). Thus \(N-1\leq r-1\), so \(r\geq N\).
Since \(r\mid N\), this forces \(r=N\), proving that \(N\) is prime.

The auxiliary numbers needed below are also prime. The numbers
\(2,3,5,7,11,23\) are prime by direct trial division. For \(641\), use
\[
641-1=640=2^7\cdot5
\]
and the base \(3\). Repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{640}\equiv1\pmod{641},\qquad
3^{320}\equiv640\pmod{641},\qquad
3^{128}\equiv357\pmod{641}.
\]
The relevant gcds are \(1\), as is explicitly witnessed by
\[
320\cdot639-319\cdot641=1,
\qquad
-9\cdot356+5\cdot641=1.
\]
Thus Lucas’s criterion, for the prime divisors \(2\) and \(5\) of \(640\),
shows that \(641\) is prime.

Similarly,
\[
277-1=276=2^2\cdot3\cdot23.
\]
Using base \(5\), repeated squaring gives
\[
5^{276}\equiv1\pmod{277},
\]
and
\[
5^{138}\equiv276,
\qquad
5^{92}\equiv116,
\qquad
5^{12}\equiv27
\pmod{277}.
\]
The required coprimality statements follow respectively from
\[
138\cdot275-137\cdot277=1,
\]
\[
53\cdot115-22\cdot277=1,
\]
and
\[
32\cdot26-3\cdot277=1.
\]
Therefore \(277\) is prime.

We can now certify \(42307\). Its predecessor factors completely as
\[
42307-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
For the base \(3\), modular exponentiation by repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and, corresponding in order to \(q=2,3,11,641\),
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(42306)/q&3^{42306/q}\pmod{42307}\\ \hline
2&21153&42306\\
3&14102&36715\\
11&3846&17937\\
641&66&10961
\end{array}
\]
The gcd of one less than each residue with \(42307\) is \(1\). Explicit Bézout
identities establishing these four assertions are
\[
21153\cdot42305-21152\cdot42307=1,
\]
\[
-12239\cdot36714+10621\cdot42307=1,
\]
\[
6088\cdot17936-2581\cdot42307=1,
\]
and
\[
-6651\cdot10960+1723\cdot42307=1.
\]
All prime divisors of \(42306\) have already been shown prime, so Lucas’s
criterion proves that \(42307\) is prime.

Finally,
\[
116341-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
For the base \(14\), repeated squaring gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and the following residues:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&116340/q&14^{116340/q}\pmod{116341}\\ \hline
2&58170&116340\\
3&38780&50801\\
5&23268&81650\\
7&16620&10889\\
277&420&35125
\end{array}
\]
Again, one less than each residue is coprime to \(116341\). This follows from
the Bézout identities
\[
58170\cdot116339-58169\cdot116341=1,
\]
\[
21846\cdot50800-9539\cdot116341=1,
\]
\[
-15490\cdot81649+10871\cdot116341=1,
\]
\[
-9200\cdot10888+861\cdot116341=1,
\]
and
\[
-9026\cdot35124+2725\cdot116341=1.
\]
Since \(2,3,5,7,277\) are prime, Lucas’s criterion proves that \(116341\) is
prime.

Thus
\[
3,37,43,42307,116341
\]
are five distinct primes. In particular they are pairwise coprime, so formula
(4) applies to their product \(n\).

### 3. Evaluation of the gcd-sum

Using (4),
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(n)
 &=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
   (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
 &=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The successive products are
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\qquad
365\cdot85=31025,
\]
\[
31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Therefore
\[
P(n)=610815156979325.
\tag{6}
\]
On the other hand, the successive products defining \(n\) are
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\qquad
111\cdot43=4773,
\]
\[
4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\]
and
\[
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051.
\]
A direct multiplication now gives
\[
26n
 =26\cdot23492890653051
 =610815156979326
 =P(n)+1.
\tag{7}
\]
Thus \(n\mid P(n)+1\). Equation (7) implies
\[
\gcd(n,P(n)+1)=\gcd(n,26n)=n,
\]
and hence
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,P(n)+1)}=\frac{n}{n}=1.
\]

It remains only to note that \(n\) is not \(1\) and is not prime. It is plainly
greater than \(1\), and it has the proper nontrivial divisor \(3\): explicitly,
\[
n=3\bigl(37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\bigr),
\]
where the second factor is greater than \(1\). Therefore \(n\) is composite.

We have consequently found a positive composite integer
\[
\boxed{n=23492890653051}
\]
for which \(a(n)=1\). This contradicts the proposed assertion that \(a(n)=1\)
only when \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime, and therefore disproves the conjecture.
